hints: Track distinct subsequences starting with each bit, counting the empty subsequence in both totals.
Prepending one bit adds the other count to its own count.
Reverse this process with Euclid?s algorithm and try all possible coprime final counts.
analogy: A binary string corresponds to a path from (1,1) using additions of one coordinate to the other.
example: The string 101 has 6 distinct nonempty subsequences; the corresponding final pair has total 8 when each category includes the empty subsequence.
algorithm: Let N=n+2. For every a from 1 to N-1 with gcd(a,N)=1, set b=N-a. Compute the number of subtractive Euclid steps needed to reduce (a,b) to (1,1), using integer division to batch repeated subtractions; keep the pair with minimum length. Re-run those subtractions, writing 1 when a>b and 0 when b>a, to construct the string. Output that shortest trace.
correctness: For a string, let a and b count distinct subsequences beginning with 1 and 0, with the empty subsequence included in each. Prepending 1 changes (a,b) to (a+b,b), and prepending 0 changes it to (a,a+b). Hence the nonempty count is a+b-2, and every string gives a unique coprime pair reachable from (1,1). Subtractive Euclid reverses these steps, so trying all pairs of total n+2 and minimizing trace length finds a shortest string.
complexity: For n up to 10^6, scanning all candidate pairs with batched Euclid takes O(n log n) time and O(log n) space for the chosen output.
